title: High-income taxes: keep the rates after 2030?

shots.narration: Proposition three is about whether existing higher income-tax rates should expire. Voters approved these rates in twenty twelve and extended them in twenty sixteen. They are now scheduled to end after twenty thirty.
shots.headline: A temporary tax reaches another decision

shots.narration: The additional rates apply to roughly the highest-earning two percent of taxpayers. This is a tax on income, such as wages or investment profits, rather than a tax on everything someone owns.
shots.headline: Income is different from wealth
items: Not a tax on total assets

shots.narration: Proposition three would make those higher rates permanent. It would keep the current system beyond its scheduled expiration, rather than introducing a new increase in everybody’s rate today.
shots.headline: What YES would change

shots.narration: Imagine a teacher planning future classes and support services.
shots.headline: Planning beyond the next school year

shots.narration: If an existing revenue stream ends, a budget planner must consider cuts, replacement taxes, or other funding. Keeping that revenue can avoid that particular gap, but does not promise any school a specific staffing level.
shots.headline: Why an expiration matters

shots.narration: School budgets depend on the wider state budget.
shots.headline: Revenue supports more than one program

shots.narration: The analyst estimates five to fifteen billion dollars of annual revenue maintained after the scheduled expiration. The wide range reflects the volatile incomes and investment gains of high earners. It is not a guaranteed fifteen billion every year.
shots.headline: A range, not a guaranteed amount

shots.narration: Roughly forty percent would support schools and community colleges. The remainder supports other state programs and reserves. Those shares describe the analyst’s estimate, rather than a promise that every dollar goes to classroom instruction.
shots.headline: Where the money would go

shots.narration: A no vote does not lower rates immediately. The scheduled expiration would still occur in twenty thirty-one. Comparing yes and no therefore means comparing future budgets, not just this year’s tax bill.
shots.headline: When the choices diverge

shots.narration: A voter might prefer protecting existing revenue for education and other services, with the additional tax concentrated on high earners. Making the rates permanent removes repeated expiration deadlines, though it does not make the revenue itself predictable.
shots.headline: The case for YES
items: Concentrate the added tax on high earners

shots.narration: You might ask whether a temporary tax should stay permanent.
shots.headline: Your question: should the tax expire?

shots.narration: A skeptical voter could want the state to honor the sunset or reduce reliance on a small, volatile tax base. They may worry about effects on investment or where high earners live. The size of behavioral effects is uncertain.
shots.headline: The case for NO
items: Question reliance on volatile high incomes

shots.narration: In the September PPIC survey of likely voters, 58 percent said yes, 40 percent no, and 2 percent were unsure. These are dated survey results, not votes already cast.
shots.headline: September snapshot: PPIC

shots.narration: A later September Berkeley survey found 54 percent yes, 34 percent no, and 13 percent undecided. Question wording and methods differ, so comparing polls does not by itself establish a trend.
shots.headline: September snapshot: Berkeley IGS
shots.poll_note: Berkeley IGS · Sept 15–20, 2026 · likely voters · about ±3 points

shots.narration: Yes makes the current higher rates permanent; no preserves their scheduled expiration. Visit our website for the fuller explanation, source links, and official voter guide. Compare the tradeoffs, then make your own informed choice.
shots.headline: Explore the full explanation
